Surah Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is Meccan, and has fifty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ ﴿A Book﴾: it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "This is a Book," meaning the surah. The clause that follows, ﴿which We have sent down to you﴾, is in the place of raf' (nominative position) as a description (sifah) of the indefinite noun (nakirah). ﴿That you may bring mankind﴾ through your supplication to them ﴿from darknesses into light﴾: from misguidance into guidance. ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾: by His facilitating and making easy (for them), a metaphor borrowed from "idhn" (permission), which is the facilitating of a barrier; this is what He grants them of success (tawfiq). ﴿To the path of﴾: a substitute (badal) for "light," with the governing particle repeated (i.e., "ila" repeated). ﴿the Mighty﴾: the Overpowering, the One who takes vengeance; ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾: the One who is praised for His bounties.

ابن: ﴿Allah﴾ with the nominative (ضمّ) is read by Madani and Shami readers, on the reading "هو اللهُ" (He is Allah). The others read it in the genitive (جرّ), taking it as an appositive (عطف بيان) to ﴿al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥamīd﴾ (the Almighty, the Praiseworthy). ﴿Who—to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in creation and dominion.

When he had mentioned those who are brought out of the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith, he threatened the disbelievers with woe (al-waylu, "wayl"), which is the opposite of al-wa'l (salvation/refuge), and it is a noun of meaning like halak (destruction). So He said: ﴿And woe to the disbelievers because of a severe punishment﴾. It is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar) and also a description (ṣifah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 3:

﴿Those who prefer﴾ (yastahibbūn) means: they choose and prefer ﴿the worldly life over the Hereafter, and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾, that is, from His religion, ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾. They seek for the way of Allah deviation and crookedness. The original construction is "wa-yabghūnahā li-hā" (and seek it for it), so the preposition was elided and the verb was made to reach its object directly. ﴿Those who﴾ (alladhīna) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿they are in far-off error﴾ from the truth. The description of error as "far" (ba'īd) is a figurative attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī); in reality, the "far" belongs to the one who errs, because it is he who distances himself from the path of truth, so the attribute was given to his action, as you say: "his effort was diligent" (jadda jidduhu). Alternatively, the phrase may be in the genitive as an attribute of "the disbelievers"; or in the accusative by way of censure (ʿalā al-dhamm); or in the nominative, meaning "I mean those who" (a'nī al-ladhīna), or "they are those who" (hum alladhīna).

﴿Never did We send a messenger except with the tongue of his people﴾, except speaking in their language, ﴿so that he might make clear to them﴾ what he was sent with and for. Then there will be no proof for them against God, and they cannot say to Him, "We did not understand what we were addressed with." If you say: Our Messenger (ﷺ) was sent to all people, as in His saying, "Say: O people, I am the Messenger of God to you all" (7:158), indeed to both the two weighty groups (al-thaqalayn, humankind and jinn), who have different tongues. If there is then no proof for the Arabs, there is proof for others. I say: It is either that the Qur'an was revealed in all tongues or in one of them. There is no need for it to be revealed in all tongues, because translation (tarjama) takes its place and suffices, avoiding prolixity. Therefore it is determined that it was revealed in one tongue, and the tongue of his people was more appropriate for that designation, because they are closer to him, and because it is further from distortion and alteration (tahrif wa tabdil).

﴿So God leads astray whom He wills﴾: whoever prefers the cause of misguidance. ﴿And guides whom He wills﴾: whoever prefers the cause of guidance. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: so He is not overcome in His will. ﴿The Wise﴾: so He forsakes none except those who deserve to be forsaken.

﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, the nine (signs), ﴿that: "Bring out your people"﴾ — with the meaning of "an" (that) being "akhrij" (bring out), or "ay" (namely): "Bring out," because sending (al-irsal) carries within it the sense of saying, as if it was said: "We sent him, and We said to him: Bring out your people ﴿from the darknesses into the light﴾, and remind them of ﴿the Days of Allah﴾," that is, warn them of His events that befell the nations before them, the people of Nuh, ʿAd and Thamud. From this is the (usage) "ayyam al-ʿArab" (the Days of the Arabs) for their wars and battles. Or (it means) the days of blessing, when He shaded them with the cloud, sent down upon them al-manna and al-salwa, and split the sea for them. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every ṣabbar﴾, (one who is) patient in trials, ﴿shakur﴾, (one who is) grateful for gifts. As if he said: "for every believer," since faith is two halves: one half is patience and one half is gratitude. (p-163)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 6:

﴿And when Musa said to his people: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Fir'awn (Pharaoh), who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord."﴾

Idh (when) is an adverbial complement (zarf) modifying "ni'mah" (favour), in the sense of "in'am" (bestowal): that is, His bestowal upon you at that time. Or it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion) for "ni'mat Allah," meaning: remember the time of your deliverance.

﴿...and they slaughtered your sons﴾: Mentioned in al-Baqarah as yudhabbihuna (slaughtering, with the waw), and in al-A'raf as yuqattilun (killing) without the waw, and here with the waw. The conclusion is that where the verb of slaughtering lacks the waw, it is made an explanation (tafsir) and clarification (bayan) of "al-'adhab" (the torment); and where the waw is affirmed, the slaughtering is treated as something that exceeded the genus of torment, as though it were a different genus.

﴿...and they kept your women alive. And in that was a tremendous trial (bala') from your Lord.﴾ The demonstrative "dhalikum" refers to the torment, and "bala'" means "mihnah" (ordeal); or it refers to the deliverance, and "bala'" means "ni'mah" (blessing).

﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 7:

﴿And when your Lord proclaimed⦆ means: He announced (āḏana). The equivalent of ta'adhdhana and ādhana is taw'ada and awʿada (he threatened). In taf'ala there must be an added meaning not present in af'ala, as if it were said: "And when your Lord announced (ādhana) with an eloquent announcement, by which doubts and suspicions are removed." This is part of what Musa said to his people, and its placement is by way of conjunction with "the favour of God upon you," as if it were said: "And when Musa said to his people: Remember the favour of God upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed." The meaning is: "And when your Lord proclaimed, saying: ﴿If you give thanks⦆, O Children of Israel, for what I have bestowed upon you of the favour of deliverance and others, ﴿I will surely increase you⦆ in favour upon favour. Thanks is the binding of what exists and the hunting of what is lost. It is also said: when a favour hears the melody of thanks, it prepares itself for increase. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "If you give thanks" by striving diligently in obedience, "I will surely increase you" by striving diligently in reward. ﴿But if you are ungrateful⦆ for what I have bestowed upon you, ﴿indeed My punishment is severe⦆ for whoever disbelieves My favour. As for in this world, it is the removal of favour; and as for in the hereafter, it is the succession of retributions. (p-164)

Moses said: "If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth together, then indeed Allah is Free of need (Ghani) from your thanks, Praiseworthy (Hamid)," even if those who praise Him do not praise Him. You have harmed yourselves, O Children of Israel, in that you have deprived yourselves of the good that you cannot do without.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 9:

﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you: the people of Noah, ʿAd and Thamud?﴾ It is either part of the speech of Musa to his people, or the beginning of an address to the people of the age of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And those after them, none knows them except Allah.﴾ This is a sentence composed of a subject and predicate, placed as a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ). Or "those after them" is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "the people of Noah," and "none knows them except Allah" is a parenthetical insertion. The meaning is that they are so numerous that none knows their number except Allah. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil there are thirty fathers who are unknown. It is also narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said upon the revelation of this verse: "The genealogists have lied." ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ with miracles. ﴿But they put their hands into their mouths﴾ The two pronouns refer to the disbelievers, meaning: they bit their fingertips with their teeth out of amazement, or they gnawed upon them out of rage. Or the second refers to the prophets, meaning: the people thrust their hands into the mouths of the messengers so that they would not speak of what they had been sent with. ﴿And they said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent, and indeed we are in grave doubt (shakk) about that to which you invite us﴾ namely, belief in Allah and monotheism (tawhid). ﴿Disquieting﴾ causing unease (rība) in the one who considers it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 10:

﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ The interrogative hamza (hamzat al-inkar, the hamza of denial) has been placed before the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), because the discussion is not about doubt itself; rather, it concerns that about which doubt is held, and that it does not admit of doubt because the proofs are evident. This is the reply to their statement: ﴿And indeed we are in doubt concerning that to which you invite us.﴾ ﴿He invites you (p-165) to faith so that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾ if you believe. The preposition "min" (some of) is not used with it except in addressing the disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿And fear Him and obey me﴾ [Nuh: 3]; ﴿He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ [Nuh: 4]; ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in Him; He will forgive you some of your sins﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. And in addressing the believers He said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce﴾ [al-Saff: 10], up to His saying ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾ [al-Saff: 12], and other instances known by inductive survey (al-istiqra', the inductive survey of usage). This was for the sake of distinguishing between the two modes of address, and so that it would not equate the two groups in the promise. ﴿And defer you to a specified term﴾: to a time that He has named and whose duration He has made clear. ﴿They said﴾, that is, the people: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾, meaning: you are nothing but, [and] there is no superiority between us and you, nor any superiority of yours over us; so why are you singled out for prophethood to the exclusion of us? ﴿You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship﴾, meaning: the idols. ﴿Then bring us a clear authority﴾: a manifest proof. Yet their messengers had already come to them with clear proofs; what they meant by "clear authority" was a sign they had proposed, out of obstinacy and contentiousness.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 11:

﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only humans like yourselves"﴾: this is a concession to their (the disbelievers') statement that they (the messengers) are human beings like them.

﴿But Allah bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants﴾: by faith and prophethood, as He bestowed it upon us.

﴿It was not for us to bring you an authority except by the permission of Allah﴾: this is a response to their statement, "Then bring us a clear authority." The meaning is that bringing the sign you have proposed is not up to us, nor within our power; rather, it is a matter that depends on the will of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾: a command from them to the believers in general to rely upon (Allah), and by it they intended themselves first and foremost, as if they were saying: "It is incumbent upon us to rely upon Allah in patience over your opposition, hostility and harm to us." Do you not see His saying...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 12:

﴿And what reason do we have not to put our trust in God?﴾ Its meaning: what excuse do we have for not putting our trust in Him, (p-166) when He has already done for us what necessitates our trusting in Him? ﴿And He has guided us to our paths﴾, namely, the granting of success (tawfiq) in guiding each of us to the way (sabil) that it is obligatory for him to follow in religion. Abu Turab said: Tawakkul is casting the body into servitude ('ubudiyyah), attaching the heart to Lordship (rububiyyah), being thankful at the time of giving, and being patient at the time of trial. ﴿And we will surely bear patiently what you have inflicted upon us﴾ is the answer to an implied oath (qasam mudmar), meaning: they swore to be patient over their harm and not to cease calling them (to faith). ﴿And upon God let those who trust rely﴾, meaning: let those who trust (in God) remain steadfast in their trust, so that it does not become mere repetition.

"And those who disbelieved said to their messengers" — "subulana" (our ways) — "li-rusulihim" (to their messengers): Abu 'Amr reads it as "li-rusulihim" [with the form rusul]. "We will surely drive you out of our land" — from our lands — "or you will return to our religion" — i.e., one of the two matters will certainly happen: either your expulsion or your return. They swore to that. The word "return" (al-'awd) is used in the sense of "becoming" (al-sayrura), and this is common in the speech of the Arabs. Or they addressed it to every messenger and those who believed with him, so the plural was given precedence over the singular in address. "So their Lord revealed to them: We will surely destroy the wrongdoers." The verb of saying is implied, or the revelation (al-iyhaʾ) is treated as having the status of speech, since it is a kind of speech.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 14:**

﴿And We will surely settle you in the land after them﴾, that is, the land of the wrongdoers and their dwellings. In a hadith: "Whoever harms his neighbour, Allah will bequeath to him his house." ﴿That﴾, the destruction and the settling, that is: that matter is true ﴿for him who fears My standing﴾, My station, which is the station of reckoning. Or "standing" is superfluous (muqham, an inserted word that adds no meaning). Or it means: fears My watch over him with knowledge, as in His saying: "Is He who is standing over every soul with what it has earned [like those who associate partners with Allah?]". The meaning is: that is a truth for the God-fearing ﴿and fears My warning﴾, My punishment. With the letter ya' (yāʾ), Yaʻqub (recites it as ﴿وَخافَ وعِيدِي﴾, with the first person).

(p-167)

﴿And they sought victory﴾, meaning they asked God for help against their enemies. This is coordinated with (ma'tuf 'ala) "He revealed to them." ﴿And every obstinate tyrant was disappointed﴾, meaning every arrogant, insolent, defiant one who turned away from the truth (mujanib li-l-haqq) was lost. Its meaning: they were helped, they prevailed, and they succeeded, and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed; and they (the tyrants) were their own people. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and its meaning is: the disbelievers sought victory over the messengers, thinking that they themselves were upon the truth and the messengers upon falsehood; and every obstinate tyrant among them was disappointed and did not prosper by his seeking victory.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 16:

﴿Behind him﴾ means from before him (min bayni yadayhi). ﴿Hell (jahannam)﴾. This describes his state while he is in this world, because he is lying in wait for Hell, so it is as if it were before him, and he is on its brink. Or it describes his state in the Hereafter, when he is resurrected and made to stand (for account). ﴿And he will be given to drink﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to an omitted element whose implied sense is: "Behind him is Hell, into which he will be cast with what he will be cast into, and he will be given to drink." ﴿from water of pus (sadid)﴾: this is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire. "Sadid" is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "ma'" (water), because the latter is indefinite (mubham), so it is clarified by the word "sadid."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 17:

﴿Yatajarra'uhu﴾ (he gulps it down) means he drinks it sip by sip, ﴿and he almost cannot swallow it﴾.

It means he does not even come close to swallowing it, so how could swallowing happen? It is like His saying, ﴿he could hardly see it﴾ (lam yakad yarāhā), meaning he did not come close to seeing it, so how could he see it? ﴿Death comes to him from every place﴾, meaning the causes of death come upon him from every direction, or from every place in his body. This is an expression of the terribleness of the pains that afflict him, as if to say: if there were any death, each of these places would be fatal for him. ﴿Yet he is not dead﴾, because if he died he would find rest. ﴿And behind him﴾, that is, before him, ﴿is a harsh punishment﴾, meaning that at every moment he faces, he receives a punishment greater and harsher than what came before it. It is also reported from al-Fudayl that it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 18:

﴿The likeness of those who﴾ is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "in what is recited to you is the likeness of those who ﴿disbelieve in their Lord﴾." The word "mathal" (likeness, parable) is used figuratively for a description in which there is strangeness. His saying ﴿Their deeds are like ashes﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumlah musta'nafah), on the assumption of a questioner who asks, "What is their likeness?" So it is said: "Their deeds are like ashes" ﴿on which the wind blows violently﴾. "Al-Riyah" (the winds) is read by Madani (a reader of the Qur'an). ﴿On a stormy day﴾: the stormy quality (al-'asf) is attributed to the day, while it actually belongs to what is in it, which is the wind, just as you say "a rainy day" (yawm mati).

The deeds of the disbelievers are the noble acts that they used to do, such as maintaining family ties (silat al-arham), freeing slaves (itq al-riqab), ransoming captives (fida' al-asra), slaughtering camels for guests (aqr al-ibil lil-adyaf), and other things. He likened their being rendered void (hubut), because they were built on something without a foundation, which is faith in God Most High, to ashes which the violent wind has scattered. ﴿They have no power﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿over anything of what they have earned﴾ of their deeds, ﴿[of] anything﴾, i.e., they will not see any trace of reward from it, just as one has no power over anything of the ashes that the wind has scattered. ﴿That is the far-off error﴾: a reference to how far their error is from the path of truth, or from reward.

Did you see that Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth? Alif-lam-mim-ra... no, correction: the passage begins with "Alam tara" (﴿Did you not see﴾), meaning: "Did you not know?" The address is to everyone. "Allah created the heavens and the earth" — "creator" (khaliq) read as an added form (idafa) by Hamza and Ali. ﴿In truth﴾ means with wisdom and a great purpose, and He did not create them in vain. ﴿If He wills, He will remove you and bring a new creation﴾ — that is, He is able to annihilate people and create in their place another creation, in their form or in a different form, to inform that He is capable of annihilating what exists and bringing into existence what does not.
﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾ — not hard to accomplish.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 21:

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, all of them.﴾ (They will come forth) — that is, on the Day of Resurrection. The verb is expressed in the past tense (wa-barazu, "they came forth") though the event is future, because what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, reports is, by its certainty, as if it has already occurred and been realized. The same applies to ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out﴾ and ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out﴾, and other such instances. As for the meaning of their coming forth before Allah, while Allah, exalted is He, has nothing hidden from Him before they come forth: they used to conceal themselves from people's eyes when committing abominations, supposing that this was hidden from Allah. Then, when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be exposed before Allah in their own selves, and they will know that nothing hidden is concealed from Him. Or it means that they come out of their graves and thus come forth to the reckoning and judgment of Allah.

﴿Then the weak (al-du'afa')⁠ (p-169)﴾ — in opinion, namely the base and the followers. The word "al-du'afa'" is written with a waw before the hamza, according to the pronunciation of those who emphasize the alif before the hamza and incline it toward the waw. ﴿said to those who were arrogant﴾ — namely the masters and leaders who misled them and turned them away from listening to the prophets and their followers: ﴿Indeed, we were to you followers (taba'an)﴾ — followers. The word tabi' is pluralized as tabaʿ, like khadim and khadam, and ghaʾib and ghayab, or as dhawu taba'. Taba' means following; one says tabi'ahu taba'an.

﴿So will you not avail us anything against the punishment of Allah?﴾ — will you be able to ward off any part of that in which we are? The first "min" (min shay') is for specification (li-l-tabyin), and the second is for partitive (li-l-tab'id), as if it were said: "Will you avail us some of that thing which is the punishment of Allah?" Or both are partitive, meaning: "Will you avail us some part of a thing which is some part of the punishment of Allah?" Since the words of the weak were a rebuke to them and a reproach for their misleading, because they knew that they could not avail them,

﴿They will say﴾ [Ibrahim: 10] to them, replying and making excuse: ﴿If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you﴾ — that is, if Allah had guided us to faith in the world, we would have guided you to it; that is, if Allah had guided us to the path of salvation from punishment, we would have guided you; that is, we would have availed you and led you along the path of salvation just as we led you along the path of perdition.

﴿It is the same for us whether we lament or are patient﴾ — equal for us are lamenting and patience. The hamza and "am" (umm) are for equalization. It is narrated that they will say in the Fire: "Come, let us lament," and they will lament for five hundred years, but lamenting will not benefit them. Then they will say, "Come, let us be patient," and they will be patient for five hundred years, but patience will not benefit them. Then they will say: ﴿It is the same for us whether we lament or are patient.﴾ Its connection to what precedes is that their reproach to them was a lamenting over what they were in; so they said to them: ﴿It is the same for us whether we lament or are patient,﴾ meaning themselves and them together, since they are united in the punishment of the misguidance in which they were united. They are saying: what is this lamenting and reproach? Lamenting is of no more use than patience.

﴿We have no place of escape (mahis)⁠﴾ — refuge and flight, whether we lament or are patient. It is also permissible that this be the speech of the weak and the arrogant together.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 22:**

﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided.﴾ It was decreed that the Garden and the Fire belong to their respective people, the reckoning was finished, and the people of the Garden entered the Garden while the people of the Fire entered the Fire. It is narrated that at that moment Satan stands up as a preacher upon a pulpit of fire and says to the people of the Fire: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth﴾, which is the resurrection and the recompense for deeds, and He fulfilled for you what He promised you. ﴿And I promised you﴾ that there would be no resurrection, no reckoning and no recompense, ﴿but I broke it to you﴾, that is, I lied to you. ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾, meaning no power or ability to dominate you, ﴿except that I called you﴾. Rather, I called you to error through my whisperings and my embellishing, and the exception here is disjunctive (munqati'), because calling is not of the same kind as authority. ﴿So you responded to me﴾, meaning you hastened to answer me. ﴿So do not blame me﴾, because whoever has openly devoted himself to enmity cannot be blamed when he calls to an ugly matter, especially when the Most Merciful has already said to you: ﴿Let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 27]. ﴿And blame yourselves﴾, since you followed me without any proof or evidence.

The statement of the Mu'tazila (al-Mu'tazila, the rationalist school that held that human beings create their own actions): this is evidence that the human being is the one who chooses wretchedness or happiness and secures it for himself, and that from God there is only enablement (al-tamkin, the granting of capacity), and from Satan only embellishment (al-tazyin), is false, because of His saying: "If Allah had guided us" (i.e., to faith) "we would have guided you," as has already been explained. ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾: none of us can rescue the other from the punishment of Allah or give him relief. The word al-israkh means al-ighatha (rescue, relief). "Bi-musrikhiyya" is read by Hamza with kasra on the ya' in order to match the kasra of the kha' (ittiba' li-l-kha', assimilation of the vowel to the preceding kha'). The rest of the readers read it with fath on the ya', so that the kasra and the two ya's do not come together after two kasras. It is the plural of musrikh, so the first ya' is the ya' of the plural and the second is the first-person pronoun (damir al-mutakallim). ﴿Indeed, I disbelieved in what you associated with me﴾. It is read with ya' by Basri, and ma is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyya). ﴿From before﴾ is related to "you associated me," meaning: I disbelieve today in your association of me with Allah from before this day, that is, in the world, like His saying: "And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your associating them" [Fatir: 14]. The meaning of his disbelief in their associating him is his disassociation from it and his denouncing of it, like His saying: ﴿We disown you and what you worship besides Allah; we have rejected you﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 4]. Or "from before" is related to "I disbelieved," and ma is a relative pronoun (mawsula), meaning: I disbelieved from before, when I refused to prostrate to Adam, in the One whom you made a partner with me, and He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. One says "ashraka-ni fulan," meaning he made me a partner to him. The meaning of their association of Satan with Allah is their obedience to him in what he embellished for them of the worship of idols. This is the last statement of Satan. His saying ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment﴾ is the statement of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is part of the speech of Iblis, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only related what he would say at that time as a kindness (lutf) to the listeners.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 23:

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ — it is coordinated (ʿatf) with "they came forth" (barazū). ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ — it is related to "will be admitted" (udkhila), meaning: the angels caused them to enter the Garden by the permission of Allah and His command. ﴿Their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾ — this is the greeting of some of them to others in the Garden, or the greeting of the angels to them.

﴿Have you not considered how Allah sets forth an example﴾: that is, He describes it and makes it clear. ﴿A good word﴾ is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: He made a good word ﴿like a good tree﴾. This is an explanation of His saying "Allah sets forth an example," like the construction "the amir honored Zayd": he clothed him in a robe and mounted him on a horse. Alternatively, "an example" (mathalan) and "a word" (kalimatan) are both objects of "sets forth" (daraba), meaning: He set forth a good word as an example, that is, made it an example. Then He said "like a good tree" as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is like a good tree. ﴿Its root is firm﴾: that is, in the earth, its roots striking down into it. ﴿And its branches are in the sky﴾: its top and its head. The good word is the word of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid): its root is affirmation in the heart (tasdiq bil-janan), its branches are declaration by the tongue (iqrar bil-lisan), and its fruit is the work of the limbs ('amal al-arkan). Just as a tree remains a tree even if it bears no fruit, so the believer remains a believer even if he does not act; but trees are only desired for their fruits, and the fuel of the Fire is only from trees when they habitually fail to bear fruit in the season of fruiting. The "tree" (shajarah) is every fruit-bearing tree with good fruit, such as the palm, the fig tree and the like. The majority hold that it is the palm tree. On the authority of Ibn 'Umar: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day: Allah has struck an example of the believer as a tree; tell me what it is. People fell to thinking of the trees of the wilderness, and I was a boy, and it came into my heart that it was the palm tree. But I was shy before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to say it, being the youngest of the people. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Indeed, it is the palm tree. 'Umar said: O my son, if you had said it, it would have been dearer to me than red camels."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 25:

﴿It gives its produce every season﴾ it gives its fruit at every time that Allah has appointed for its bearing, ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾ by the facilitation and creation of its Creator, ﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people, that they may remember﴾, because in the setting forth of parables there is greater understanding, reminder, and depiction of the meanings.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 26:

﴿And the likeness of an evil word﴾ is the word of disbelief, ﴿like an evil tree﴾ is every tree whose fruit is not good. It is reported in a hadith that it is the colocynth tree (shajarat al-hanzal). ﴿It is uprooted from above the earth﴾ means its whole trunk (juthth) is torn out entirely. The true meaning of al-ijtithath (uprooting) is taking the whole body (juththah) of the tree, while its root is in opposition to it, i.e., it remains fixed. ﴿It has no stability﴾ means no istiqrar (settledness). It is said: qarra al-shay'u qararan, like your saying thabata thabatan (the thing became firm). The likeness of this is the statement that is not supported by proof; it is refuted and not firm.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 27:

﴿Allah firmly establishes those who believe﴾, i.e., He keeps them steadfast upon it. ﴿with the firm word﴾, which is the saying: "There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." ﴿in the life of this world﴾, so that when they are tried in their religion they do not slip, as those who were tried by the People of the Trench (ashab al-ukhdud) and others remained firm. ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾. The majority hold that this refers to the grave, through the prompting of the answer and the enabling of the right response. On the authority of al-Bara', that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the taking of the soul of the believer, and said: "Then his soul is returned to his body, and two angels come to him and seat him in his grave, and they say to him: 'Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?' He says: 'My Lord is Allah, my religion is Islam, and my Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ).' Then a caller calls out from the heaven: 'My servant has spoken the truth.' That is His saying: ﴿Allah firmly establishes those who believe with the firm word﴾. Then the two angels say (p-173): 'You lived happily, you died praised, sleep the sleep of the bride.'" ﴿And Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾, so He does not keep them firm upon the firm word in the situations of trials, and their feet slip at the first thing, and in the Hereafter they are more astray and more prone to slipping. ﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾, so there is no objection to Him in firmly establishing the believers or leading the wrongdoers astray.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 28:

﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah﴾, i.e., the thanks for the favor of Allah, ﴿for disbelief﴾, because the thanks that was obligatory upon them, they put in its place disbelief. So it is as if they changed thanks into disbelief and substituted it entirely. They were the people of Makkah, whom Allah honored with Muhammad (ﷺ), but they disbelieved in the favor of Allah instead of the thanks that was incumbent upon them. ﴿And caused their people﴾ who followed them in disbelief ﴿to alight in the abode of perdition﴾, the abode of destruction.

﴿Jahannam﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan, a noun that clarifies the preceding noun). ﴿They will enter it﴾ means they will enter it. ﴿And wretched is the abode﴾ means and wretched is the resting place, which is Jahannam.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 30:

﴿And they set up rivals to God﴾ — equals (amthal) in worship, or in naming (al-tasmiyah). ﴿So that they may lead astray from His way﴾ — with a fatha on the ya' it is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr (layudillu, i.e. "so that He may lead astray" is the reading with the ya' vowelled with fatha, meaning they caused others to stray). ﴿Say: Enjoy yourselves﴾ — in this world; and what is meant by it is abandonment (al-khidhlan) and being left to yourselves (al-takhliyah). Dhu al-Nun said: "Enjoyment (al-tamattu') is that the servant fulfils whatever he is able of his desire." ﴿For indeed your destination is to the Fire﴾ — your return is to it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 14, verse 31:

﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾: He specified them by attributing them to Himself (*idafah*, possessive attachment) as an honour. The yā' is read with sukūn by Shāmī, Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and al-Aʿshā. ﴿that they establish the prayer and spend of what We have provided them﴾: The object of the speech is omitted, because "say" (*qul*) requires something said. That something is "establish" (*aqīmū*), and its full form is: "Say to them: Establish the prayer and spend, that they may establish the prayer and spend." It has also been said that the content is a command in the jussive form, with the estimate "that they may establish and that they may spend" (*li-yuqīmū wa-linunfiqū*), so the lām of command (*lām al-amr*) was deleted because *qul* indicates it. Had it been said directly, "they establish the prayer and spend" (*yuqīmū al-ṣalāh wa-yunfiqū*), without the lām, it would not be permissible. (p-174) ﴿secretly and openly﴾: Both words are in the accusative. They may be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), meaning "those with secrecy and openness," i.e. secretly and openly. They may be an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), meaning "at times of secrecy and openness." Or they may be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning "spending in secret and spending openly." The meaning is to conceal voluntary charity and to make obligatory charity known. ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trading nor friendship﴾: That is, there is no benefit in it through trade or through friendship. *Khilāl* means friendship (*mukhāllah*). Benefit on that Day comes only from spending for the sake of Allah. Makkī and Baṣrī read both words with fatḥah, while the rest read them with ḍammah and tanwīn.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 32:

﴿Allah﴾ is the subject (mubtada') ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾ is its predicate (khabar). ﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾: from the clouds, rain. ﴿So He brought forth thereby fruits as a provision for you﴾. "From the fruits" (min al-thamarat) is an explanation (bayan) of "provision" (rizq), meaning: He brought forth thereby a provision which is fruits. Or "from the fruits" is the object (maf'ul) of "brought forth," and "provision" (rizqan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 33:

﴿And He subjected for you the ship, to run in the sea by His command; and He subjected for you the rivers﴾ [Ibrahim: 32] ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant﴾. "Constant" means lasting, and it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the sun and the moon, meaning: they persevere in their course, in their giving of light, in their driving away of darknesses, and in their bringing about what they bring about of good for the earth, for bodies, and for plants. ﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day﴾, succeeding one another in alternation, for your livelihood and your rest.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 34:

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him.﴾ "Min" (from) here is partitive, meaning: He gave you some of the totality of what you asked of Him. Or, reading "and He gave you of every" as "thing you asked for and what you did not ask for," then "ma" is a descriptive (ma mawsufah), the clause is its qualifier, and the second clause has been omitted because the remaining part indicates the omitted, like His saying ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. "Min kullin" is related from Abu 'Amr. And "ma sa'altumuhu" is a negation, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: He gave you of all of that without your asking for it. Or "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), meaning: and He gave you of all of that which you needed, so it is as though you had asked for it, or requested it through the tongue of circumstance (lisan al-hal).

﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl: 18], meaning you cannot manage to count it or reach its end. This is when they wish to count it in summary; as for its detail, none knows it but Allah.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ever a wrongdoer﴾ who wrongs the favour by neglecting to thank it, ﴿a great ingrate﴾, intensely ungrateful for it. Or: "wrongdoer" in hardship, who complains and panics; "ingrate" in favour, who hoards and withholds. "Al-insan" is generic, so the statement about wrongdoing and ingratitude encompasses whoever possesses them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 35:

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ — Remember when Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, make this land﴾ — that is, the Sacred Land (al-Balad al-Haram), ﴿secure﴾ — possessing security. The difference between this and what is in al-Baqarah is that there he asked that it be made among the towns whose people are safe, whereas here he asked that it be removed from the attribute of fear to security, as if he said: "It is a land that inspires fear, so make it secure."

﴿And keep me away﴾ — and distance me; that is: make me firm and constant in avoiding their worship, as he said, ﴿and make us submitting to You﴾, that is: keep us firm in Islam. ﴿And my sons﴾ — he meant his offspring from his loins. ﴿That we worship idols﴾ — from worshipping idols.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 36:

﴿My Lord, they have indeed led many of the people astray﴾. They were described as "leading astray" by way of causation (al-tasbib), because the people went astray on account of them, so it is as though they themselves led them astray. ﴿Whoever follows me﴾ in my religion (millah), being upright (hanif) and submitting (muslim) like me, ﴿then he is of me﴾, that is: he is a part of me, because of the intensity of his special closeness to me. ﴿And whoever disobeys me﴾ in matters short of shirk, ﴿then You are indeed Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Or: whoever disobeys me with the disobedience of shirk, then You are indeed Forgiving and Merciful if he repents and believes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 37:

﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring﴾ — some of my children, namely Isma'il and those born of him — ﴿in a valley﴾ — this is the valley of Makkah — ﴿without cultivation﴾ — where nothing of crops has ever existed at all — ﴿by Your Sacred House﴾ — this is the House of Allah, so named because Allah, exalted is He, forbade violating it and treating it lightly, and made the area around it a sanctuary (haram) for its sake. Or it is so named because it has always been protected, so that every tyrant stands in awe of it. Or because it is respected, of great sanctity, whose sanctity may not be violated. Or because it was made forbidden to the Flood, meaning it was protected from it, just as it is called "ancient" (ʿatiq) because it was freed (u'tiqa) from [domination]. ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾ — the lam is connected to "I have settled," meaning: I have only settled them in this barren valley so that they may establish prayer by Your Sacred House and make it flourish with Your remembrance and worship. ﴿So make hearts among people incline toward them﴾ — hearts from among the hearts of people. The min here is partitive (lil-tab'id), according to what is related from Mujahid: "Had he said 'the hearts of people,' Persia, the Romans, the Turks and the Indians would have crowded you for it." Or it is for commencement (lil-ibtida'), like your saying: "The heart from me is sick," meaning "my heart." So it is as if it were said: "hearts of some people." He made the genitive noun indefinite in this illustration to match the indefiniteness of "hearts" (afidah), since in the verse it is indefinite, so that it encompasses some of the hearts. ﴿Yearning toward them﴾ — hastening to them from distant lands and flying toward them in longing. ﴿And provide them with fruits﴾ — despite their dwelling in a valley in which there is nothing of them, by having them brought to them from distant lands. ﴿That perhaps they may give thanks﴾ — for the blessing of being provided with all kinds of fruits in a valley in which there is neither tree nor water.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 38:

﴿Our Lord﴾: the repeated address (al-nida', "calling out") is evidence of humble supplication (al-tadarru') and seeking refuge (al-laja') in God. ﴿Indeed You know what we conceal and what we reveal﴾: You know the secret just as You know the open. ﴿Nothing is hidden from God, on earth or in heaven﴾: this is either from the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim (peace be upon him), or from the words of Ibrahim, and "min" (from/any) here is for comprehensiveness (li'l-istighraq), as if it were said: "Nothing whatsoever is hidden from God."

"Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age (ʿalā al-kibar), Ismaʿil and Ishaq." Here ʿalā is in the sense of maʿa (with), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: He granted me while I am old.

"Ismaʿil and Ishaq." It is narrated that Ismaʿil was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old. It is also narrated that Ismaʿil was born to him when he was eighty-four, and Ishaq when he was ninety.

He mentioned the state of old age because the favour of granting a child at that time is greater, since it is a state in which despair of having children has set in, and attaining a need after despair is among the greatest blessings. Also, birth at that advanced age was a sign (āyah) for Ibrahim.

"Indeed my Lord is All-Hearing of supplication" (innā rabbī la-samīʿ al-duʿāʾ), meaning One who answers supplication (mujīb al-duʿāʾ). This is from your saying: "The king heard the speech of so-and-so" when he received it with acceptance and approval. From this comes: "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (samiʿa Allāh li-man ḥamidah). He had called upon his Lord and asked for a child, saying: "My Lord, grant me of the righteous" (Rabb hab lī min al-ṣāliḥīn), so he thanked Allah for the honour of His answering him.

The idafa of samīʿ to al-duʿāʾ is an idafa of the adjective to its object; the original form is la-samīʿun al-duʿāʾa. Sibawayh mentioned faʿīl among the patterns of intensive nouns (abniyat al-mubālaghah) that work like verbs, as in your saying: "This is raḥīmun abāhu" (one who is very merciful to his father).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 40:

﴿My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and [make] from my offspring [such]﴾ "and some of my offspring" is in the accusative as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the object in ﴿make me﴾ (ijʿalnī). He made it "some" (baʿḍa) because he knew, through Allah's informing him, that there would be disbelievers among his descendants. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "There will always be people among the descendants of Ibrahim upon the fitrah (the natural disposition to faith) until the Hour is established."

﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾ with the yāʾ (the final "ī" of duʿāʾī) in both continuation (waṣl) and pause (waqf) is read by Makki, and Abu ʿAmr and Hamza agree with him in continuation. The rest read it without the yāʾ. The meaning is: answer my supplication, or my worship.

﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you call upon besides Allah﴾ [Maryam: 48].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 41:

﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾, i.e., Adam and Eve; or he said it before the prohibition and the despair regarding the faith of his parents; ﴿and the believers on the Day when the Reckoning takes place﴾, i.e., it is established; or the standing (qiyam) of its people is attributed to the Reckoning by metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), like "and ask the town" (wasal al-qaryata).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 42:

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do.﴾ This is a consolation for the oppressed and a threat to the oppressor. The address is to someone other than the Messenger (peace be upon him); and if it is addressed to the Messenger, then the purpose is to strengthen him (peace be upon him) in his state of not thinking that Allah is unaware, like His saying ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [Yunus: 105], and ﴿And do not call upon another god along with Allah﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]; and as occurred in the command ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa: 136]. It has also been said that its purpose is to make known (al-iedhan) that He knows what the wrongdoers do, and nothing of it is hidden from Him, and that He will punish them for its little and its much, by way of warning and threat (al-wa'id wa al-tahdid), like His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾ (p-178)

﴿He only defers them﴾, i.e., their punishment, ﴿to a Day when eyes will stare fixedly﴾, i.e., their eyes will not remain still in their places from the terror of what they see.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 43:

﴿Muhti'een﴾ hastening towards the caller ﴿Muqni'i ru'usihim﴾ raising their heads ﴿la yartaddu ilayhim tarfuhum﴾ their gaze does not return to them, so that they look at themselves; ﴿wa af'idatuhum hawa'un﴾ their hearts are empty of good, and do not comprehend anything out of fear. Al-hawa' (the void, emptiness): the empty space that bodies do not occupy; it is applied to this, so it is said: "the heart of so-and-so is hawa'" when he is a coward, having no strength or boldness in his heart. And it is said: they are hollow, having no minds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 44:

﴿And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾, i.e., the Day of Resurrection. "The Day" (yawm) is the second object (maf'ul thani) of "warn" (andhir), not an adverbial of time (zarf), since warning does not take place on that Day. ﴿Then those who did wrong will say﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿"Our Lord, grant us respite for a brief term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers."﴾ That is: return us to the world and give us respite for a short span and limit of time, so that we may make up for what we neglected of answering Your call and following Your messengers. Then it will be said to them, ﴿"Did you not swear before that you would have no end [to your life]?"﴾ That is: you swore in the world that when you died you would not be removed from that state and would not be transferred to another abode, meaning you disbelieved in resurrection, as in His saying, ﴿And they swore by God with their strongest oaths that God will not raise up those who die﴾ [al-Nahl: 38]. And "what you have" (ma lakum) is the answer of the oath. It came in the form of direct address, as in His saying "you swore" (aqsamtum); had it reported the words of the swearers, it would have said "what we have" (ma lana min zawal). Alternatively, "the Day" may mean the Day of their destruction by the immediate punishment, or the Day of their death, when they are tormented by the severity of the agonies of death and by the meeting of the angels without good tidings. For on that Day they will ask their Lord to delay them to a brief term.

It is said: "He dwelt in the house" (sakana al-dara) and "he dwelt in it" (sakana fihā). From this comes the verse ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾ by disbelief. This is because al-sukna (dwelling) derives from al-sukūn, which means staying and remaining. The original construction is that it takes fī, as in qarra fī al-dār (he settled in the house) and aqāma fīhā (he resided in it). However, when it was transferred to a specific sense of sukūn, it was used with its object directly, so it was said sakana al-dāra, just as it was said tabawwaʾahā (he occupied it).

It is also possible that sakanū derives from al-sukūn, meaning: they settled there and were at ease, with contented hearts, following the course of those before them in wrongdoing and corruption, not relating to others what the earlier peoples suffered in the days of Allah and how the outcome of their wrongdoing was, so that they might take warning and be restrained. ﴿And it became clear to you﴾ through reports or through direct observation. The subject of tabayyana (it became clear) is an implied pronoun indicated by the context, meaning: their condition became clear to you. And ﴿how﴾ (kayfa) is not the subject, because the interrogative does not take what precedes it as its operator; rather, kayfa is in the accusative by the words ﴿We did to them﴾, meaning: We destroyed them and took vengeance upon them. ﴿And We struck for you the parables﴾, meaning: the descriptions of what they did and what was done to them. These are, in their strangeness, like the parables struck for every wrongdoer.

﴿And they had indeed plotted their plot﴾, meaning their great plot, in which they exhausted their effort, which is what they did in supporting disbelief and nullifying Islam. ﴿And with Allah is their plot﴾. It is annexed (*mudaf*) to the agent, as the first was, and the meaning is: their plot is recorded with Allah, so He will requite them for it with a plot greater than theirs. Or it is annexed to the object, meaning: "and with Allah is their plot, by which He plots against them," and this is their punishment, which will come upon them from where they do not perceive. ﴿And though their plot was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾, read with a kasra on the first lam and a fatha on the second. The estimate is: "even if their plot occurred to remove the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ)." He expressed the Prophet (peace be upon him) by the mountains because of the greatness of his station. The verb *kāna* (كانَ) is either complete (*tāmmah*), meaning "occurred," or *in* is negative and the lam is emphatic for it, as in His saying ﴿And Allah would not punish them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. The meaning is: it is impossible that the mountains be moved by their plot, on the basis that the mountains are a metaphor (*mathal*) for the signs of Allah and His laws, because they are like firm mountains in steadiness and establishment. Its evidence is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, "وَما كانَ مَكْرُهُمْ", and the recitation with a fatha on the first lam and a raised second lam, which is that of ʿAlī, meaning: "and though their plot was" of such severity that the mountains would be moved by it and uprooted from their places. Then *in* is the light (*mukhaffafa*) form of *inna*, and the lam is emphatic.

﴿So do not think that Allah would break His promise to His messengers﴾, meaning His saying ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] and ﴿Allah has decreed: "I will surely prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21]. "Mukhlif" (breaking) is the second object (maf'ul thani, the second object of the verb) of "tahsabanna" (do think). He made "mukhlif" modify "wa'dihi" (His promise), which is the second object of "mukhlif," while "rusulahu" (His messengers) is the first object. The underlying sense is "mukhlif rusulihi wa'dahu" (breaking the promise to His messengers). He placed the second object before the first only to make clear that He does not break a promise at all, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9]. Then he said "rusulahu" (His messengers) to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, how then would He break it to His messengers, who are His chosen ones and His elite? ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty﴾, prevailing, not to be outwitted, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾ against His enemies on behalf of His allies.

The phrase ﴿on the day the earth is changed into another earth, and the heavens﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*, ظَرْف) governed by "the retribution" (lil-intiqam), or it is governed by an implied verb, "remember" (*idmar*, إضمار, "an omitted verb understood from the context"), so that the sense is "Remember the day...". The meaning is: on the day this earth that you know is changed into a different earth, unlike this known one, and the heavens are changed into other heavens. The verb is omitted because what precedes it indicates it.

*Al-tabdil* (التبديل, "substitution, alteration") means change. It may apply to essences, as when you say, "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars" (بَدَّلْتُ الدَراهِمَ دَنانِيرَ), or to attributes, as when you say, "I changed the ring into a seal" (بَدَّلْتُ الحَلْقَةَ خاتَمًا) when you melt it down and reshape it into a seal, moving it from one form to another.

Scholars differ concerning the change of the earth and the heavens. It is said that their attributes are changed: the mountains are removed from the earth, its seas are made to burst forth, and it is levelled so that you see in it no crookedness or elevation. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (رضي الله عنهما) that it is the same earth, but it is altered and changed. As for the heaven, it is changed and substituted by the scattering of its stars, the eclipsing of its sun and moon, its splitting open, and its becoming gates. It is also said that another earth and other heavens will be created in their place. It is related from Ibn Masʿud (رضي الله عنه) that people will be gathered upon a white earth on which no one has committed a sin. It is related from ʿAli (رضي الله عنه) that the earth will be changed into silver and the heavens into gold.

﴿And they will come forth﴾ (وَبَرَزُوا), meaning they will emerge and come out of their graves, ﴿before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ (لِلَّهِ الواحِدِ القَهّارِ). This is like His saying: ﴿"Whose is the dominion today?" "It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer."﴾ [Ghafir: 16], because when dominion belongs to one who is overpowering and cannot be overcome, and no one can seek help from anyone other than Him, the matter reaches its utmost severity.

And you will see the criminals — the disbelievers — on that Day, the Day of Resurrection, bound together in pairs (muqarranin). They are linked together: some with others, or with the devils; or their hands are bound to their feet, shackled (mughallalin) (p-181) in chains (al-asfad). The phrase "fi al-asfad" (in chains) is related to "muqarranin": that is, they are bound together in chains. Or it is not related to it, and the meaning is: bound together, fettered. Al-asfad are shackles or fetters.

﴿Their garments﴾ their shirts ﴿of pitch﴾ is what exudes from a tree called al-abhal (the Himalayan/ wild pine-like tree), which is boiled, and with it mangy camels are daubed. Its sharpness and heat burn away the mange. It is a substance in which fire quickly spreads. It is black in colour and foul-smelling, so the skins of the people of the Fire are daubed with it until their coating becomes for them like garments, so that the sting and burning of the pitch, the rapid spread of the fire over their skins, and the dark colour and foul smell all gather upon them. The difference between the two pitches is like the difference between the two fires. Everything that God has promised or threatened in the Hereafter, the distance between it and what we witness of its kind is beyond measure, as if what we have of it is only the names, while the realities are there. We seek refuge in God from His wrath and His punishment. "مِن قِطْرٍ آنٍ" (from molten copper), Zayd, from Ya'qub: molten copper whose heat has reached its utmost limit. ﴿And the fire covers their faces﴾ rises over them as it blazes. He specified the face because it is the most honoured place on the outer body, like the heart within it, and for this reason He said ﴿which mounts over the hearts﴾ [al-Humazah: 7].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 14, verse 51:

﴿That Allah may recompense every soul for what it has earned﴾. That is: He does with the wrongdoers what He does, so that He may recompense every wrongdoing soul for what it has earned, or every soul, whether wrongdoing or obedient. For when He punishes the wrongdoers for their wrongdoing, it becomes known that He rewards the believers for their obedience. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: He takes account of all the servants in less time than the blink of an eye.

This (ʾay: that which He described in His words, "And do not think" [Ibrahim: 42] up to His words, "swift in reckoning" [Ibrahim: 51]) is a message (balagh) for mankind, a sufficiency in reminding and admonition. "And that they may be warned by it" — by this message. It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to an omitted clause, meaning: "that they may be advised, and that they may be warned." "And that they may know that He is only one God" — because when they fear what they have been warned of, fear leads them to reflection until they arrive at tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), for fear (khashyah) is the mother of all good. "And that those of understanding (ulu al-albab) may take heed," meaning those who possess intellects (dhawu al-uqul).
